title: More Japanese Seniors Are Starting Businesses
paragraphs: Japan is getting older. Around 30% of the country's population is now 65 or over — one of the highest percentages in the world.
But for many Japanese people, getting older doesn't mean leaving work behind.
A government report from this year found that nearly 40% of people aged 65 and over would like to keep working. And in 2025, a record 9.3 million people in this age group were still working.
But some are going even further — by starting businesses of their own.
Research company Teikoku Databank found that people aged over 60 started more than 20% of the companies founded in Japan in 2025. That was the highest percentage since records began in 2000.
The number of business loans from Japan Finance Corporation for companies started by people 60 and up has also more than doubled over the past five years.
For Chizuko Fukatsu, the idea for her business came from her own experience.

While buying clothes for her mother, Fukatsu saw there were very few good options for women in their 80s and older. So, in her 60s, she started the clothing company Fukufuku-Ya, creating clothes that are both stylish and practical for elderly women.
Fukatsu had never worked in the clothing industry before and had to learn everything from scratch.

And as more seniors start businesses, the need for support is also growing. Mari Tanimura, who works for a free business support center in Osaka, told NHK that while many older people may have strong technical skills, they often need help with things like raising money and sales.
Experts say seniors should start with a low-risk business idea that requires little money and few employees, and then grow slowly from there.
